newsitem.title: FRANCE: Ireland's Bruton defends EU reform document.
newsitem.headline: Ireland's Bruton defends EU reform document.

text.p: Irish Prime Minister John Bruton on Tuesday defended his country's attempts to draft a pact on European Union reform against French criticism that the document was not ambitious enough.
Bruton, in Paris to meet President Jacques Chirac, said France had a key role in drafting the document it criticised.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette had complained bitterly on Friday that the draft did not go far enough in reforming EU institutions.

"I praised the role Mr Barnier (French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier)...had actually played in helping us to draft the document," Bruton, whose country is the current holder of the rotating EU presidency, told a news conference after meeting Chirac.
"It is important to make the point that the document produced by Ireland represented work by Mr Barnier," he said.
De Charette had said the draft "mirrors the mediocrity of the negotiations so far". He also asked: "Do we want to work together in the EU?"

Bruton said the document, designed as a working paper for an eventual EU treaty to be approved next June at the end of the impending six-month Dutch presidency, was comprehensive and he questioned whether de Charette had read the full text before making his remarks.

"I have the report of what everyone else had to say about our draft and I wouldn't want to embarass the people involved, but everyone was highly complementary...I hope Mr de Charette actually read the document before he made his comments," Bruton said.
De Charette's comments were sharply at odds with views expressed by other governments including those of Germany, Italy and Britain, all of which praised Ireland's work.
He said the document did not settle disagreements on a few issues such as majority voting and the composition of the European Commission.

"Rather than produce a text that would be to say the least inelegant we decided to produce, on that limited range of issues, a discussion of the problems with possible solutions without treaty text," Bruton said.
"I know it's a very good document. I think it's a credit to the people involved in it, including Mr. Barnier," Bruton said.
